samples.summary: The `t` clamp does not do what it claims: a forged future timestamp still wins the line label forever
samples.evidence: `sanitizeWrittenAt` clamps a client-supplied `t` to `now`, where `now = Date.now()` is taken at READ time (yorkie-note-store.ts:161) on every call to `getAuthorSpans()`. A hostile run written with `t: 4e15` therefore reports `at === now` on every read, while every genuine run reports its real (strictly earlier) write time. `authorOfRange` (packages/notes/src/view/blame-gutter.ts:48) picks the span with the maximum `at`, so the forged run outranks every genuine edit on its line at every read, indefinitely — including edits made after the forgery, because those too are compared against a re-read `now`. This is exactly the outcome the code comment (lines 56-61) and docs/design/notes/notes.md:582-585 assert is prevented ("it becomes a tie that document order breaks"). It only becomes a tie for edits written in the same millisecond as the read. Attack: attach to the note's Yorkie doc (or just call `content.edit` from a patched client), insert one character anywhere on a target line with `{a:'victim', t: 4e15}`, and that line is permanently attributed to `victim` for every collaborator. The new test at yorkie-note-store.test.ts:243 only asserts `at <= Date.now()`, which the ineffective clamp satisfies, so the suite reads as covering a control that is not working. An added-but-ineffective mitigation is worse than none, because the doc now records the risk as bounded.

samples.summary: `sanitizeAuthor` strips only Cc/Cf, so several classic invisible-character spoofs survive; the 64-char slice can also split a surrogate pair
samples.evidence: The stated goal (line 44-48, and notes.md:583-586) is that "a forged name cannot render as somebody else's through invisible characters, nor break the gutter out of its one-line column". `/[\p{Cc}\p{Cf}]/gu` covers C0/C1 controls, ZWSP and the bidi formatters, but not: U+3164 HANGUL FILLER, U+115F/U+1160 (category Lo, render as blank), U+FFA0, U+2028/U+2029 (Zl/Zp line/paragraph separators), or combining marks (Mn) used for Zalgo overflow. A hostile client can therefore still write `aㅤnn` and have the gutter render a label visually identical to `ann`, defeating the mitigation's stated purpose. Additionally `.slice(0, MAX_AUTHOR_LENGTH)` cuts at a UTF-16 boundary and can leave a lone surrogate at the end of the displayed label. Impact is bounded (the gutter is a reading aid and the label is set via `textContent`, so no XSS), but the documented guarantee is stronger than the code delivers.

samples.summary: Sanitization of untrusted author strings lives in one store implementation, not at the rendering trust boundary that consumes them
samples.evidence: `authorOfRange`/`BlameMarker` accept whatever string a `NoteStore.getAuthorSpans()` returns and put it straight into `span.textContent` and `span.title` (blame-gutter.ts:105,112). The only sanitization is inside `YorkieNoteStore.getAuthorSpans()` in packages/frontend. `packages/notes/src/store/memory.ts:117` returns `mark.author` verbatim, and the `NoteAuthorSpan` contract in packages/notes/src/store/store.ts:113 documents no sanitization obligation, so a second store implementation (or a future non-Yorkie backend) silently reintroduces the untrusted-name path. Placing the strip/cap in `computeBlameLabels` (or documenting it as a contract precondition on `NoteAuthorSpan.author`) would make the guard non-bypassable rather than per-implementation.

samples.summary: Peer-controlled presence `color` is interpolated raw into a CSS style attribute (same untrusted-presence boundary this change documents as handled)
samples.evidence: `attributes: { style: \`background-color: ${peer.color}\` }` uses `peer.presence.color` (yorkie-note-store.ts:429), a value any attached client sets for itself and which nothing validates. A hostile peer can set `color` to `red; background-image: url(https://attacker/beacon?d=1)` (or `content`/`background` tricks) to inject arbitrary declarations into the victim's editor DOM — remote resource loading and presence beaconing without JS execution. This line predates the delta, but the delta newly writes a trust-boundary note (yorkie-note-store.ts:20-40, docs/design/notes/notes.md:565+) asserting that the untrusted-presence blast radius is enforced, which makes the unvalidated sibling field on the same presence object worth naming. Fix: validate against the `hsl(...)` shape `noteUserColor` produces, or fall back to a default.

samples.summary: Label computation is quadratic in attacker-controllable run count, giving a cheap client-side DoS on every collaborator
samples.evidence: `authorOfRange` rescans the span array from index 0 for every line, so `computeBlameLabels` costs O(lines x spans) and runs on every doc-changing update (blame-gutter.ts:141). `YorkieNoteStore.getAuthorSpans()` emits one span per CRDT run, and a hostile client controls run count directly: writing each character with a distinct `t` attribute forces one run per character, so spans ~ document length and the walk becomes quadratic in note size on every keystroke, on every peer's main thread. Nothing caps span count or memoizes per-line lookup. Mitigating factors: the gutter is off by default and must be enabled per user. A binary search / cursor over the sorted spans, or a span-count cap, removes the amplification.

samples.summary: Note presence broadcasts the signed-in user's email to every attached client, including anonymous share-link visitors
samples.evidence: `initialPresence` publishes `email: currentUser.email` into the Yorkie note presence, which every attached client (including an anonymous `role: 'viewer'` share-link visitor, per yorkie-auth.controller.ts:196-200) can read via `getOthersPresences()`. Predates this delta, but the delta's new trust-boundary section enumerates what crosses this exact boundary and omits it; if the section is to be the record of the note presence trust model, an email address leaving the workspace to anonymous visitors belongs in it (or the field should be dropped from presence, since only `username`/`photo`/`color`/`name` are needed by the avatar chrome and carets).

finding.summary: The `t` clamp does not do what it claims: a forged future timestamp still wins the line label forever

It only becomes a tie for edits written in the same millisecond as the read. Attack: attach to the note's Yorkie doc (or just call `content.edit` from a patched client), insert one character anywhere on a target line with `{a:'victim', t: 4e15}`, and that line is permanently attributed to `victim` for every collaborator. verdict.reason: The described code exists exactly as claimed and the mechanism holds. `sanitizeWrittenAt` (yorkie-note-store.ts:63-68) clamps with `Math.min(value, now)` where `now` is captured at READ time (yorkie-note-store.ts:161) and applied to every run (line 177). A run forged with a far-future `t` therefore reports `at === now` on every call, while genuine runs report their write-time `Date.now()` (yorkie-note-store.ts:146), which is strictly smaller on any later read. `authorOfRange` (blame-gutter.ts:42-49) selects the span with maximum `at`, so the forged run wins the line label on every read, permanently, including against edits made after the forgery — the opposite of the "becomes a tie that document order breaks" claim in the code comment (lines 55-61) and docs/design/notes/notes.md:582-585. No other guard normalizes or re-clamps `t`: `getAuthorSpans()` is the only reader of the attribute and `authorOfRange` the only consumer of `at`. The test at yorkie-note-store.test.ts:233-245 asserts only `at <= Date.now()`, which the ineffective clamp satisfies, so the control reads as covered while not functioning. No refutation ground applies: the code is present, unguarded, and this is a documented anti-spoofing mitigation that does not work, making persistent impersonation of line authorship possible for any attached client.

finding.summary: Blame attribution is derived entirely from client-controlled presence with no server-side verification, so any editor can forge another user's authorship
finding.evidence: `localAuthorName()` reads `this.doc.getMyPresence()?.name` (yorkie-note-store.ts:135) — a value the client itself set at attach time (notes-detail.tsx:259, shared-document.tsx:890). Presence content is never validated: I found no server-side check of presence or of `Text` attributes (yorkie-auth.controller.ts only authorizes doc key + verb; yorkie-event.controller.ts has no username/identity handling; note-content.ts ignores attributes). A malicious client with write access — including an *anonymous* share-link visitor, since yorkie-auth.controller.ts:200 grants `rw` to `link.role === 'editor'` with no login — can call `presence.set({ name: 'victim-username' })`, or write the attributes directly as `content.edit(from, to, text, { a: 'victim-username', t: Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER })`. Because `authorOfRange` picks the run with the largest `at` (blame-gutter.ts:48) and `t` is a client-supplied `Date.now()`, a forged far-future timestamp lets an attacker permanently own the displayed author of any line they touch by one character — e.g. insert a space into a victim's line, or attribute their own defamatory text to the victim. The gutter presents this as fact ("who last edited each line", editor.ts:122) with no trust indicator; homoglyph/RTL-override or zero-width names sharpen the impersonation (`author.trim() === ''` only catches pure whitespace, blame-gutter.ts:51). Mitigating: docs/design/notes/notes.md explicitly calls blame "a reading aid, not an audit trail" — but that caveat is not surfaced in the UI. Amplifier, pre-existing and out of diff: the auth webhook runs in shadow mode unless `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE === 'true'` (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:86-105), so today even the editor-role gate is not enforced.

verdict.reason: The finding's security impact rests on three specific gaps, and each already exists as an enforced guard in the tree. (a) Timestamp forgery: sanitizeWrittenAt clamps client-supplied `t` to `Date.now()` and maps invalid values to 0 (yorkie-note-store.ts:63-68), applied on the read path at yorkie-note-store.ts:177, so a far-future `t` cannot outrank genuine edits — it becomes a tie broken by document order (blame-gutter.ts:48); tested at yorkie-note-store.test.ts:233-245. (b) Invisible-character impersonation: sanitizeAuthor strips all \p{Cc}\p{Cf} (zero-width, bidi overrides, control) and caps length at 64, applied to attributes written by ANY client on read (yorkie-note-store.ts:50-53, 176); tested at yorkie-note-store.test.ts:247-264. (c) "No trust indicator in the UI": the gutter marker renders the hover title `${label} (self-reported)` (blame-gutter.ts:103-114). Additionally, an exhaustive grep for getAuthorSpans/NoteAuthorSpan/AUTHOR_ATTR shows the only consumer is the gutter label computation (blame-gutter.ts:132,143) — blame is never an input to an access decision, never persisted server-side, and the trust boundary is documented as intentional (yorkie-note-store.ts:20-40; docs/design/notes/notes.md:567-592). What is left is that display names in a collaborative editor are client-set (normal for Yorkie/CodePair presence) and homoglyph look-alikes remain possible: a hardening nit on a display-only reading aid, not a blocking authorization/crypto/injection defect under the security rubric. The separately-cited shadow-mode webhook flag (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:86-105) is a different subject from this finding's claim.
